messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Insurance Agent
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 39

Arthur is nine when the glass jar slips from his small hands and shatters against the kitchen tiles. Before the shards finish settling, his mother crosses the narrow hallway. Her jaw tightens, the familiar premonition of violence already radiating from her shoulders. He learns to make himself smaller, to keep his breathing shallow, to read the micro-tensions in her posture before they escalate into strikes. The first blow catches his ribs; the second sends him stumbling backward into the sideboard. He survives by anticipating the storm, by cataloguing every shift in her mood, by mapping the geography of danger in the few rooms they share. That early calculus of threat becomes his lifelong architecture. In his teens, he masters the art of quiet observation. He avoids crowded hallways, keeps his head down, and memorizes exit routes in every building he enters. By his early twenties, he seeks a profession where outcomes can be measured, where risk is quantified, where decisions rest on documented facts rather than unpredictable moods. He becomes an insurance agent. He builds his practice on precision, learning to trace the lineage of a claim, to spot the discrepancy in a policyholder’s statement, to anticipate gaps in coverage before they become disasters. Colleagues praise his thoroughness. Clients trust his caution. What they do not see is the constant internal ledger, the way he files away every interaction for hidden liabilities, the way he keeps his voice level even when his pulse hammers against his collarbone. Now, at seventy-one, Arthur lives alone in a quiet condo two blocks from his office. He has never married. His days follow a strict routine: morning review of pending claims, midday calls with underwriters, afternoon policy revisions. The work satisfies him because it offers structure, a clear boundary between what is documented and what is not. Yet the past does not stay filed. Some afternoons, a dropped stapler makes his shoulders lock rigid. A sudden knock on the conference room door sends his heart into a frantic rhythm against his sternum. He tells himself it is only age, only the body’s slow decay, but his muscles remember the weight of a heavy hand, the metallic taste of fear, the way stillness was the only armor. He avoids the building’s basement archive, preferring the stairwell. He declines invitations to group dinners, citing paperwork, though the real reason is the exhaustion of masking his hypervigilance in a crowded room. When he lies in bed, he rehearses conversations that will never happen, checking every sentence for fault, for blame, for the chance to rewrite what cannot be changed. The afternoon light shifts across his polished oak desk. Arthur picks up his pen. The claim form remains unfinished. He breathes slowly, deliberately, counting the spaces between the ticks of the wall clock. Outside, a car horn blares. He does not flinch this time. He watches the sound dissipate into the street, waits for the quiet to settle, and turns the page.
